operations.hypothesis: An execute_sql argument whose exact schema identifiers carry a space, punctuation or a reserved word is repaired by backtick-quoting those identifiers only (literals and already-quoted regions untouched), and an assistant turn that serialised its native call as <tool_call> XML text is converted into a real tool_calls entry; both remove the failure before the environment sees it while leaving every other turn byte-identical.

Grounding the solver in the exact public table and column names (schema card appended once to the system message, plus a quoting reminder in the execute_sql description) stops respellings such as HockeyGames/Acting and stops unquoted spaced names from ever being emitted, without changing any tool name, schema or order.

A public-history monitor that counts failed execute_sql results per statement text and emits one concrete remediation hint (at most twice per episode) breaks the observed verbatim retry loops that exhaust the 15-turn budget.

A cold-start skill that states the quoting rule, forbids invented names and CREATE TABLE, forbids verbatim retries, asks for batched INSERTs and requires commit_final_answer prevents the first avoidable error and the long recovery tails in multi-row tasks.

rounds.bundle_hypothesis: Most DBBench losses come from the emitted SQL text, not from the plan: exact public schema names that contain a space, punctuation or a reserved word (Rank, Pick #, Distance (km), Hockey Games, Acting Roles, Acting Work History) are sent unquoted, the server answers 1064/1146/1054, and the solver either retries the identical statement until the turn budget dies or misreads the missing-table error as a missing schema and creates a table. Repairing the emitted identifiers with the public schema at H2, grounding the exact names at H3, breaking repeated-failure stalls at H4 and stating the quoting/no-retry discipline at H5 should convert those episodes into single-shot successes while leaving already-correct statements byte-identical.
